the duration of postischemic hypoperfusion after TCI was prolonged and that there was no correlation between the duration and magnitude of postischemia hypoperfusion and mortality or neurologic deficit.

there is no correlation between the cerebral blood flow and the recovery after the total cerebral ischemia.

the effects of total cerebral ischemic episodes of 11 min in duration in the dog, and the correlation between cerebral blood flows and eventual survival and neurologic recovery.

no correlation between cerebral blood and neurologic recovery was found.
the results of this study do not support the concept that improved blood flow is a necessary condition for recovery of function after TCI.
the correlation between cerebral blood and oxygen delivery during the initial period after TCI and the eventual recovery of the animal was negative.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there was no correlation between blood flow and outcome.
the brain can survive 11 min of complete ischemia, and the recovery of function depends on the integrity of the blood-brain barrier.
the brain has an ability to protect itself against ischemic insult and that this ability is related to the duration and severity of the insult.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cerebral blood flow during the first 24 h after ischemia is not a good predictor of outcome, and it is not a good measure of the severity of ischemia or the extent of injury.
the brain is a complex organ and that we should not be surprised that there is not a simple linear relationship between cerebral blood flow after ischemia and recovery.
there is no correlation between the magnitude or duration of postischemic hypoperfusion and the neurologic deficit or survival.
